459.title: LLM Inference Benchmark Explorer
459.content: Compare the inference performance of different LLM, hardware and serving configurations in one place. Use the filters to select the configurations you want to compare; the table updates automatically when you change the concurrency level or your performance targets. Expand any row to view the detailed results for that configuration. How to use the benchmark explorer

460.title: What a row is
460.content: A row is one deployment configuration: a model, on specific hardware, in a specific number format, served by a specific engine with a specific parallelism and speculative-decoding setting, measured end to end. The same model therefore appears in several rows, and two rows are directly comparable only once you know which of those settings differ between them.

461.title: Filters and targets do different jobs
461.content: Filters decide which rows you see. The model, parameter-count, device, quantization and speculative-decoding filters, and the TPS, TTFT and capacity sliders, only show or hide rows. Targets and assumptions decide what the numbers say. They sit under Performance Targets and Capacity Assumptions. Changing one leaves the rows in place but recalculates Max C, both capacity columns and the green and red colouring of every row.

462.title: 1. Choose a concurrency level
462.content: Concurrency (C) is the number of requests the system is working on at the same moment. The selector picks which measurement the TPS and TTFT columns show: C=1 is the best case a single request sees, and higher values show the system under load. Rows not measured at the selected level are hidden, so the list shortens as C rises.

463.title: 2. Narrow and sort
463.content: Filters combine, and every column sorts. The most instructive comparisons change a single setting: the same model at FP8 and at NVFP4, the same configuration with and without speculative decoding, or vLLM against SGLang on the same hardware.

464.title: 3. Set your targets
464.content: Two targets define acceptable speed: a maximum TTFT (default 1000 ms) and a minimum TPS per request (default 20 tok/s). A measured level counts as supported only when it meets both; a value exactly on a target passes. TTFT matters most where someone waits for the reply to start, as in chat. TPS matters most for long answers, where the wait is spread over the whole reply. To see what a TPS value feels like, the preview under the targets streams sample text at that rate.

465.title: 4. Read Max C and the capacity columns
465.content: Max C is the highest measured concurrency that meets both targets. It counts simultaneous requests. A plus — 64+ — means the run met both targets even at the highest level it was tested at, so its real maximum was not reached. Chat Capacity and Agentic Capacity turn that into a number of people and check it against memory. Each shows the smaller of two estimates, and the icon beside the figure says which one set it: . | a lightning bolt — the speed targets; | a memory chip — the KV cache memory; | a warning triangle — the chosen context length is longer than the model can hold. | . A plus on a capacity figure — 256+ — follows from a Max C with a plus: speed set the figure, but the speed limit was never reached, so the figure is a minimum. Sorting and the minimum-capacity filters use the number itself. Hover over a figure for a one-line reason. What the numbers mean and how they are calculated, below, explains both estimates in full.

466.title: 5. Open a row
466.content: Click a row to see: . | the full concurrency sweep, marked PASS or FAIL against your targets at every level; | a speed preview for any measured level, so C=1 and C=32 can be compared by eye; | a chart of per-request TPS, the speed each user sees, against aggregate TPS, what the system produces in total — the trade-off capacity planning sits between; | a short capacity summary: what each limit allows and how much memory is left for the KV cache; | the run’s notes: cache precision, kernels, memory settings, speculation depth. | . The chart downloads as a PNG for reports and presentations.

467.title: Where to start
467.content: “We want to run this model for an agentic workload used by 20 people.” Select the model and set the minimum Agentic Capacity to 20. Keep the default targets for a first estimate, or set them to your application. What remains are the candidate hardware and serving configurations. “How does this model do on DGX B300 versus DGX Spark?” Select the model and both device families, then compare rows whose quantization, engine, speculative decoding and parallelism match. Changing the concurrency shows how the gap develops under load. “What does quantization, speculative decoding or the engine actually change?” Hold the model and hardware fixed and compare the rows that differ in that one setting, so the effect is not mixed with a hardware change. “We already own this hardware; what can we run on it?” Start with the device filter, sort the remaining models by capability or size, and narrow with the TPS, TTFT or capacity you need. “Which model is capable enough without exceeding our limits?” Sort by Intelligence Index, Agentic Index or parameter count to shortlist models, then apply your device and performance requirements. This keeps choosing a model separate from sizing the infrastructure, instead of assuming the fastest model is the most suitable. What the numbers mean and how they are calculated

468.title: How the numbers were measured
468.content: Every TPS and TTFT figure was measured with the open-source CordatusAI LLM Benchmark Tool on NVIDIA DGX B300, one to eight DGX Spark nodes, RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell and Jetson AGX Thor. Each configuration is run with 128 input tokens and 128 output tokens, ten rounds per concurrency level with prompts on different topics, at C = 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64. The table shows the mean of the ten rounds. A token is the unit a model reads and writes, about three quarters of an English word.

469.title: The measured columns
469.content: TPS (tokens per second) — how fast one request’s reply is produced at the selected concurrency. It is a per-request figure: at C=8, each of the eight requests receives this rate. The system’s total output is aggregate TPS = C × TPS, shown in the expanded row. Higher is better. TTFT (time to first token) — how long a request waits before its first token arrives. It includes time spent queueing and the prefill, the pass in which the model reads the whole prompt. Lower is better.

470.title: The columns that describe the setup
470.content: Parameters — the total number of weights in the model. For a mixture-of-experts model this is the total, not the part active for each token, because all of it has to be held in memory. Intelligence Index and Agentic Index — capability scores published by Artificial Analysis; higher is better. The first combines evaluations of reasoning, coding, science and long-context work; the second measures multi-step work with tool calls. Both describe the model, so every row of one model carries the same pair, whatever the hardware. Where several reasoning-effort settings are scored, the highest is shown, and a dash means no score has been published. The values are from Intelligence Index v4.3, retrieved on 28 September 2026. Scores from different index versions are not comparable — v4.2 and v4.3 added harder tasks, so every model scores lower than it did under v4.1 — and some older models have no v4.3 Agentic Index yet. The Agentic Index measures what the model can do; Agentic Capacity, further along the row, estimates how many people the hardware can serve. Quantization — the number format the weights are stored in. Fewer bits per weight means less memory and usually more speed, at some risk to output quality. BF16 and FP16 are full precision; FP8 and MXFP8 use 8 bits per weight; NVFP4, MXFP4, FP4, INT4 and AWQ use 4. Inference engine — the server software that loads the model and schedules requests, such as vLLM or SGLang. The same model on the same hardware can perform measurably differently under two engines. Speculative decoding — the model drafts several tokens ahead and checks them in one pass; the accepted tokens are kept, so the same output arrives sooner. The column shows whether a run used it; the mechanism and how far ahead it drafted are in the row’s notes. TP / DP / PP — how the model is split across GPUs or machines. Tensor parallelism (TP) divides the work inside each layer, pipeline parallelism (PP) places different layers on different devices, and data parallelism (DP) runs several complete copies, each serving its own requests.

471.title: Max C
471.content: Max C is the highest measured concurrency at which mean TTFT and mean TPS both meet your targets. Only measured levels count, nothing is interpolated, and if no level passes Max C is 0. It depends on your targets and moves with them: the same row may reach C=16 at 20 tok/s and only C=8 at 30 tok/s.

472.title: From requests to people: the capacity columns
472.content: Max C counts requests running at the same moment. The capacity columns estimate how many people a configuration can serve. A system can run out of speed or of memory first, so each column takes the smaller of two limits: . capacity = min(speed limit, KV cache memory limit) .

473.title: The speed limit
473.content: speed limit = floor(Max C × usage multiplier) . A person does not have a request running all the time. A chat user sends a message, waits for the reply, then reads and types for a while, and uses no capacity in between. The usage multiplier is the number of people who, on average, share one request slot. The chat default of 4 assumes a chat user has a request running about a quarter of the time. The agentic default of 1.5 assumes an agent has one running about two thirds of the time, because it chains calls while it plans, runs tools and checks results. With Max C = 8, that is 8 × 4 = 32 chat users or 8 × 1.5 = 12 agentic users.

474.title: The KV cache memory limit
474.content: While it works through a conversation, a model keeps a KV cache: for every token so far, the intermediate results each layer needs so that earlier tokens do not have to be processed again. The cache grows with the length of the conversation. The speed figures come from 128-token prompts, and a real turn is that quick only if the user’s conversation is still in the cache, so that just the new message has to be processed. The memory limit therefore counts how many users’ whole sessions fit in the cache at once. A session is as long as the context length set under the assumptions — every token it holds, history and replies included: 16K by default for chat, 64K for agentic work, whose sessions also carry tool calls and their results. Beyond that number the system still runs, but a returning user waits while their conversation is processed again. It is worked out per device — per GPU, or per node on DGX Spark: . | Memory for the engine = device memory × Engine Memory Allocation: 95% on a discrete GPU (DGX B300, RTX PRO 6000), 85% on unified memory (DGX Spark, Jetson Thor), where the operating system shares the same pool. | Room for weights and cache = that × Weights and KV Cache Share (90%). The other 10% is working memory for activations and runtime buffers. | Free for the KV cache = that − the weights held on this device: the size of the checkpoint the run served, divided over the TP × PP devices it is split across. | One session = context length × the model’s cache per token, stored at FP8 (one byte per value), plus any fixed per-session part the model has (see below), divided over the devices that share it. | Users = floor(free memory ÷ one session) × the number of DP copies. | . The cache per token comes from the model’s published configuration. For a standard transformer it is 2 (a key and a value) × layers × KV heads × head size. Worked example. A hypothetical 32-layer model with 8 KV heads of size 128, served as a 32 GB FP8 checkpoint on one 96 GB GPU: . | memory for the engine: 96 × 95% = 91.2 GB; room for weights and cache: 91.2 × 90% = 82.08 GB | free for the KV cache: 82.08 − 32 = 50.08 GB | cache per token: 2 × 32 × 8 × 128 = 65,536 bytes, so 50.08 GB holds 764,160 tokens | chat: 764,160 ÷ 16,384 = 46 sessions; agentic: 764,160 ÷ 65,536 = 11 | . With Max C = 8 the speed limit is 32 chat and 12 agentic users, so the table shows 32, set by speed, and 11, set by memory. Tighten TTFT until Max C falls to 4 and the speed limit becomes 16 and 6: both are then set by speed.

475.title: How different model designs are handled
475.content: Models differ in what they keep for each token, so every row uses its own model’s figures. For example: . | Sliding-window layers keep only their most recent tokens — the last 128 or 1,024, say — so they cost a fixed amount per session instead of growing with it. | Linear-attention and Mamba layers keep a fixed-size state instead of a per-token cache, counted once for each session. | Compressed caches, such as the MLA of DeepSeek, Kimi and GLM-5, store far less per token, but every GPU holds a full copy, so adding GPUs does not divide them. | A standard cache is split across GPUs by its KV heads; with more GPUs than heads, the heads are copied rather than split further. | . Some rows show only the speed limit, and the expanded row says why: either the served checkpoint alone is larger than the memory assumed to be available — the run gave the engine more memory than the standard allocation, or kept part of the model or its cache in CPU memory or on disk — or the model stores its cache in a way this estimate does not model. Choose a context length longer than a model’s own context window, the most it can hold, and the model cannot serve sessions that long at all: its capacity shows a dash with a warning triangle.

476.title: Reading the results at longer prompts
476.content: The TTFT target applies directly to 128-token prompts. With longer prompts, TTFT rises roughly in proportion to their length, because the prefill work grows with the prompt. TPS falls more slowly: the main cost of producing each token, the weight-matrix multiplications, does not depend on the prompt’s length, although attention and cache reads do grow with the context.

477.title: What the numbers do not tell you
477.content: The table uses one fixed workload, mean values, simple usage multipliers and a standard memory calculation, so that configurations can be compared without first building a traffic model. It is not a substitute for a production load test: tail latency, varied prompt and output lengths, arrival patterns, agent call chains and prefix sharing all change real capacity. The memory limit is calculated, not read from the engine. Engine-specific storage details — block rounding, scale factors, separate cache pools, experts spread across data-parallel devices — can move it either way. A session holding 16K or 64K tokens will also see a longer TTFT and a somewhat lower TPS than these 128-token measurements. Capacity is most meaningful where a full concurrency sweep stands behind it; a row measured only at C=1 rests on a single data point. Planned refinements include workload filters, speed measured at longer contexts, and capacity estimates based on measured latency, user think time and Little’s Law. | Intelligence Index and Agentic Index values are published by Artificial Analysis and are reproduced here with attribution. 479.title: 1. Brief Summary
479.content: Quantization lets LLM weights — and, where needed, activation/KV cache data — be represented at a lower precision (numeric representation width, i.e. bit width), reducing memory consumption, memory bandwidth demand, and, on suitable hardware, computation cost. Once seen mostly as “the compromise you reach for when the model does not fit in memory”, it is now the case that formats like FP8 and FP4 are accelerated in hardware on modern GPUs. Many model developers also release official, pre-quantized checkpoints directly. But quantization by itself does not mean “lower bits = faster”. The right choice sits at the intersection of four factors: . Workload × Quantization format × GPU architecture × Checkpoint reliability .

480.title: Three core rules
480.content: 1. If the model owner ships an official quantized checkpoint, evaluate that first. That does not automatically make it the highest-quality checkpoint; but in terms of quantization method, format and target runtime it is usually the most reliable starting point. 2. The format must match the GPU architecture. For example: . | Ampere → INT4/INT8-based methods | Ada → FP8 | Hopper → FP8 | Blackwell → FP8 / NVFP4 / MXFP4 | . A format merely “running” without native Tensor Core support does not mean it runs fast. 3. The original model’s benchmark is not the quantized checkpoint’s benchmark. The BF16 model’s score must not be assumed valid for the same model’s FP8 or FP4 checkpoint. For a quantized checkpoint, also check: . | the quantization method used, | the calibration process, | the benchmark results, | the runtime, | the GPU, | the generation settings | .

481.title: 2. What Does Quantization Buy You?
481.content: Quantization has three fundamental effects: . | Model weights get smaller | Memory bandwidth demand drops | Low-precision Tensor Core computation is accelerated on suitable hardware | . How much each matters depends on the workload.

482.title: 2.1 Memory consumption
482.content: In the ideal case, weight memory is roughly: . Parameter count × bytes/parameter . For example: . | Precision (bit width) | Bits | 7B | 70B | 405B | . | BF16 / FP16 | 16 | ~14 GB | ~140 GB | ~810 GB | . | FP8 / INT8 | 8 | ~7 GB | ~70 GB | ~405 GB | . | 4-bit | 4 | ~3.5 GB | ~35 GB | ~202 GB | . These are only ideal weight sizes. Actual GPU memory is the sum of: . Weights + KV Cache + activations + runtime overhead + quantization metadata . Also remember that in MoE models the total parameter count and the active parameter count differ.

483.title: 2.2 KV Cache quantization is a separate decision
483.content: Weight quantization and KV cache quantization are not the same thing. For example: . BF16 weights + BF16 KV BF16 weights + FP8 KV FP8 weights + FP8 KV NVFP4 weights + FP8 KV NVFP4 weights + NVFP4 KV . are entirely different deployment profiles. With long context and high concurrency, the KV cache can consume a serious amount of GPU memory. For that reason: . Weight quantization + KV Cache quantization . must be considered together. FP8 KV cache can roughly halve KV memory on a suitable runtime and model architecture; but its effect on attention quality must be verified for the model and implementation at hand. “It is a significant memory optimization for long context; the effect on model quality must be checked.” .

484.title: 3. Why Does Quantization Improve Performance?
484.content: The fundamental purpose of quantization is to reduce memory consumption and data movement by representing model weights at a lower precision, and — where the hardware and kernel support exist — to raise computation throughput. An LLM’s inference performance can be bounded roughly by two fundamental resources: . | Memory bandwidth: how fast the GPU can move model weights and other data | Compute throughput: how fast the GPU can perform matrix math with accelerator units like Tensor Cores | . Quantization can give an advantage at both points.

485.title: 3.1 Memory Bandwidth Advantage
485.content: When model weights are held at a lower precision, the model gets smaller. For a model of roughly 70B parameters, for example: . | Precision (bit width) | Approximate weight size | . | FP16 / BF16 | ~140 GB | . | FP8 / INT8 | ~70 GB | . | 4-bit | ~35 GB | . This shrinkage does not only help VRAM capacity. Since inference requires the GPU to move model weights through memory, smaller weights mean less memory traffic. This can matter especially at low concurrency and in decode-heavy workloads, because when producing a single token, reading the weights from memory can cost a significant amount compared with the computation done on them. Simplified: . Lower bits → smaller model → less data movement → higher throughput potential in memory-bound workloads . Actual throughput, however, depends on the kernel design, batch size, KV cache, GPU architecture and runtime. A theoretical memory-bandwidth calculation must therefore not be treated as real inference throughput.

486.title: 3.2 Compute Throughput Advantage
486.content: On modern GPUs the advantage of low-precision formats is not only about moving less data. A GPU’s Tensor Cores perform high-speed matrix math in specific precision formats. If the quantization format used is accelerated at the hardware level, lower precision can also mean higher computation throughput. For example: . | FP16/BF16 → high-precision Tensor Core math | FP8 → lower precision and high Tensor Core throughput | FP4/NVFP4 → very high low-precision Tensor Core throughput on architectures like Blackwell | . That is why FP8 or FP4 can bring a significant advantage even when the workload is compute-bound. In short: . Quantization does not just shrink the model; where the hardware support exists, it also taps the GPU’s higher low-precision compute capacity.

487.title: 3.3 The Effect of Concurrency and Batch Size
487.content: As concurrency and batch size grow, more tokens are processed in parallel on the same model. The GPU’s Tensor Cores are then fed better, and the share of compute throughput in total performance can grow. So the source of the quantization advantage can vary by workload: . | Workload | Main advantage of quantization | . | Single user / low concurrency | Less memory traffic | . | Medium-high concurrency | Memory + compute advantage | . | Large batch / high throughput | Tensor Core compute throughput rules | . | Compute-bound workload | Low-precision Tensor Core throughput | . | Memory-bound workload | Moving less data | . Quantization, with the right hardware and software support, can both reduce memory bandwidth demand and raise inference throughput by using the GPU’s low-precision compute capacity.

488.title: 4. GPU Architecture and Quantization Format
488.content: A quantization format must not be judged on its own. The performance of the same precision format can differ significantly across GPU architectures. The fundamental reason is that GPUs support low-precision formats at different levels.

489.title: 4.1 Why Does Hardware Support Matter?
489.content: A format making model weights smaller is no guarantee of high performance by itself. Consider two different situations: . Situation A — accelerated directly by the hardware . Quantized weights ↓ Native GPU Tensor Core ↓ High throughput . Situation B — extra conversion / custom kernel required . Quantized weights ↓ Dequantization / conversion ↓ FP16/BF16 compute ↓ Extra cost . In the second case the model may use less VRAM, but the full compute advantage expected may not materialize. So quantization selection must ask not only: . “How many bits?” . but also: . “How is this format computed on my GPU?” .

490.title: 4.2 General Approach by GPU Generation
490.content: | GPU architecture | Notable precision support | General approach | . | Ampere | FP16/BF16, INT8/INT4 | INT4/INT8 quantization and optimized kernels are strong choices | . | Ada Lovelace | FP16/BF16, FP8 | FP8 and low-bit quantization can be evaluated | . | Hopper | FP16/BF16, FP8 | FP8 is a strong native acceleration option | . | Blackwell | FP16/BF16, FP8, FP4/NVFP4 | FP8 and especially NVFP4 are significant options | . The point here is not to say “a new format will not run on an older GPU”. Software/runtime support may allow different formats to be used. But native Tensor Core support can make a decisive difference in performance.

491.title: 4.3 FP8: The Balanced Choice Between Memory and Compute
491.content: On architectures like Hopper and Blackwell in particular, FP8 combines two important advantages: . | Lower model memory than FP16/BF16 | Hardware-accelerated high Tensor Core throughput | . FP8 is therefore not just a format for squeezing the model into VRAM. Especially in high-concurrency, throughput-focused inference systems: . Lower memory footprint + higher low-precision compute throughput . can be had together. One of FP8’s important advantages over 4-bit formats is its higher numeric precision. When preserving quality is critical and the model suits FP8 well, it can be a strong preference.

492.title: 4.4 FP4 / NVFP4: The Hardware Advantage on Blackwell
492.content: With the Blackwell architecture, FP4-class formats have become more important. NVFP4 in particular must not be judged merely as a “4-bit model”. The format’s purpose is to combine the memory advantage of narrow bit widths with Blackwell’s low-precision Tensor Core support. NVFP4 can therefore help in two directions: . The memory side . FP16 → FP8 → FP4 ↓ ↓ ↓ Less model memory Less data movement . The compute side . FP16/BF16 ↓ FP8 ↓ FP4 / NVFP4 ↓ Blackwell low-precision Tensor Core throughput . So when NVFP4 is on the table on Blackwell, it is not enough to say: . “The model uses less VRAM because it is 4-bit.” . The point that matters is: . NVFP4 can bring an advantage in both memory-bound and compute-bound workloads by combining low memory use with Blackwell’s native low-precision compute capacity.

493.title: 4.5 The Basic Rule of Quantization Selection
493.content: When choosing a quantization format, four factors must be weighed together: . 1. Model quality . How much of the model’s accuracy, perplexity and task-level performance survives quantization? . 2. Memory footprint . What load do the model and the KV cache put on GPU memory? . 3. Hardware acceleration . Does the GPU support this precision format natively through Tensor Cores or another dedicated accelerator? . 4. Runtime / kernel support . How efficiently does vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, llama.cpp or whatever inference stack you run execute this format? . The format with the lowest bit count is therefore not automatically the fastest. The right choice: . is made by weighing model quality + memory footprint + native hardware acceleration + runtime/kernel support together.

494.title: 5. Quantization Formats
494.content: | Format / method | Typical use | Main advantage | . | GGUF | llama.cpp / CPU+GPU | Flexibility, broad hardware support | . | GPTQ | NVIDIA inference | Widespread weight-only quantization | . | AWQ | NVIDIA inference | Activation-aware weight quantization | . | EXL2 | NVIDIA / ExLlama | Quality-speed trade-off with variable bpw | . | INT8 / SmoothQuant | Inference | Strong option when moving to low precision | . | NF4 / bitsandbytes | QLoRA / fine-tuning | Training / fine-tuning ecosystem | . | FP8 | Ada / Hopper / Blackwell | Native low-precision acceleration | . | NVFP4 | Blackwell | Very low memory + native FP4 acceleration | . | MXFP4 | Blackwell and supporting platforms | Open MX standard, aimed at portability | .

495.title: 6. “4-bit = 4-bit” Is Not True
495.content: Two quantization methods with the same nominal bit width may give different quality or performance. For example: . INT4 AWQ GPTQ NF4 MXFP4 NVFP4 . all fall in the “4-bit” class, yet these can differ: . | number representation, | scaling, | block size, | calibration, | weight-only / weight+activation approach, | kernel, | hardware acceleration | . Hence: . “4-bit model” . is not a sufficient technical definition on its own. A more accurate definition: . “NVFP4, a Blackwell-optimized 4-bit floating-point format using 16-element micro-block FP8 scaling” . should include the format’s details like this.

496.title: 7. Why Is NVFP4 Different?
496.content: NVIDIA NVFP4 is the 4-bit floating-point format designed for Blackwell. Its basic approach is: . FP4 values + FP8 micro-scale + FP32 tensor-level scale . In NVFP4, FP4 values are scaled with an FP8 scale over 16-element micro-blocks. A tensor-level FP32 scale is used as well. This approach aims to reduce quantization error compared with a plain FP4 representation. According to data published by NVIDIA, NVFP4 can give a model footprint about 1.8× smaller than FP8 and about 3.5× smaller than FP16; the actual checkpoint size depends on the metadata and the mixed-precision recipe used. So: . NVFP4 = not just “4 bits”. The real difference is the combination: . 4-bit representation + fine-grained scaling + hardware acceleration .

497.title: 8. GPU Architecture × Format Matching
497.content: This is one of the most important decision points. | GPU architecture | Preferred options | Note | . | Pascal | GGUF Q4/Q5/Q6 | No modern FP8/FP4 Tensor Core features | . | Turing | INT8 / INT4-based methods | No native FP8 Tensor Core support | . | Ampere | INT4 / INT8, AWQ/GPTQ | A100 supports native INT4/INT8 Tensor Cores | . | Ada | FP8, INT4 | Native FP8 Tensor Core support | . | Hopper | FP8 | FP8 + Transformer Engine is a strong choice | . | Blackwell | NVFP4 / FP8 / MXFP4 | Native FP4 and FP8 acceleration | . “Preferred” here does not mean the format is automatically best for every model. Model, runtime and workload must still be evaluated.

498.title: 9. Ampere: Do Not Confuse INT4 with FP8
498.content: Ampere matters especially for this reason: . A100 / RTX 30 ↓ Native INT4 / INT8 Tensor Core ↓ AWQ / GPTQ / Marlin-style INT4 deployments . The A100 has INT4 Tensor Core support. FP8, by contrast, is a precision that came into its own with Hopper and is also supported on Ada. So on Ampere one must not assume: . “There is an FP8 file, so it must be faster.” . A runtime may execute an FP8 checkpoint in some form; but native hardware acceleration and software-level support are not the same thing. For 4-bit deployments on Ampere: . AWQ/GPTQ + a suitable optimized kernel . is the more sensible starting point in most cases.

499.title: 10. Ada and Hopper: FP8’s Strong Position
499.content: Ada Lovelace offers FP8 Tensor Core acceleration. Hopper takes FP8 further with the Transformer Engine. So: . Ada → FP8 is a serious option Hopper → FP8 is a strong default for production inference . But one must not claim: . “FP8 is always 2× faster than FP16.” . Numbers like 2× can express theoretical or peak advantages under specific kernel/throughput conditions. Real LLM throughput varies with model architecture, batch, sequence length and runtime.

500.title: 11. Blackwell: FP8 or NVFP4?
500.content: On Blackwell the central question is no longer just: . “Can I reduce the model to 4-bit?” . The better question is: . “For this model, which suits better in quality, memory and throughput: FP8 or FP4?” .

501.title: FP8
501.content: Advantages: . | higher numeric precision | generally lower quantization error | native Blackwell acceleration | a strong option in quality-critical workloads | .

502.title: NVFP4
502.content: Advantages: . | lower weight footprint | lower memory traffic | native Blackwell FP4 acceleration | the advantage of fitting larger models into smaller GPU clusters | .

503.title: Practical approach
503.content: FP8 ↓ Benchmark ↓ NVFP4 ↓ Benchmark ↓ Compare quality + latency + throughput + VRAM . The outcome: . Quality difference acceptable → NVFP4 Quality critical → FP8 . This decision must be made model by model.

504.title: 12. Mixed-Precision Quantization
504.content: Modern quantized checkpoints often do not store all weights in the same format. For example, a recipe like this may be used: . MLP → NVFP4 Attention → FP8 lm_head → NVFP4 / higher precision critical layers → higher precision . The basic rationale is: . Not every layer is equally sensitive to quantization error. A good quantization pipeline can therefore proceed like this: . Model ↓ Calibration ↓ Layer sensitivity analysis ↓ Mixed-precision recipe ↓ Quantization ↓ Benchmark . So saying only: . “The model is 4-bit.” . is not enough. What really matters is: . | which layers were quantized? | which precision was used? | what is the block size? | how was scaling done? | what is the calibration dataset? | what is the calibration algorithm? | .

505.title: 13. Why Does Calibration Matter?
505.content: During PTQ (Post-Training Quantization), the calibration dataset should represent the model’s real usage distribution. For example, choices like these make more sense: . General chat model → general text calibration Coding model → coding-weighted calibration Agent model → tool-use / instruction / reasoning calibration . The calibration process can influence where and how quantization error arises. Hence: . Same model + same 4-bit format ≠ same quality .

506.title: 14. How to Choose a Reliable Quantized Checkpoint?
506.content: When choosing a quantized model, the reliability of the source is critical.

507.title: Preference order
507.content: 1. The model owner’s official checkpoint . This is the best starting point. 2. The checkpoint released by the hardware / inference vendor . For example, NVIDIA Model Optimizer-based checkpoints whose benchmark and calibration details are given openly. 3. Quants prepared by the framework / inference community . They can work well; but the metadata and benchmark quality must be checked separately.

508.title: 4. Community-produced quantization
508.content: Quantization files prepared by the community must not be used in production without verifying their source and production process. The risk here is not only poor quantization quality. A quantized model file must not be considered reliable without verifying: . | who produced it, | which base model it was derived from, | with which quantization method and tools it was created, | which calibration data was used, | whether the integrity of the model file is preserved, | whether it is compatible with the runtime and kernels in use | . Especially in production systems, models and quantization artifacts of unknown origin become a supply-chain risk. Since model weights and their related files are the fundamental inputs of the inference pipeline that runs them, a reliability decision must not be made from a benchmark score alone.

509.title: Known publishers — a starting list
509.content: The accounts below are starting points that stand out for their production process and model card transparency. A publisher’s name is not a quality guarantee; it indicates where to begin the search: . | Publisher | Type | Typical formats | Link(s) | . | NVIDIA (Model Optimizer) | Hardware / production vendor | NVFP4, FP8 (mixed recipe) | HF nvidia · TensorRT-Model-Optimizer | . | RadixArk | SGLang ecosystem | NVFP4, blockwise FP8, MLX 4-bit, DSpark draft | HF RadixArk · cookbook.sglang.ai | . | Inferact | vLLM ecosystem | NVFP4, MXFP4, W4A4, EAGLE3 / DSpark draft | HF Inferact · inferact.ai | . | Red Hat AI | Inference provider | FP8, INT4 (AWQ/GPTQ) | HF RedHatAI | . | Intel | Hardware / runtime vendor | INT8 / INT4 | HF OpenVINO · HF Intel · neural-compressor · openvino | . | ggml-org | Format ecosystem (llama.cpp) | GGUF | HF ggml-org | . | ISTA-DASLab | University research lab — source of GPTQ, SparseGPT, AQLM, QuIP# | GPTQ / MatGPTQ, NVFP4 (MoESQ), GGUF (GSQ-RCO), 2-bit (AQLM / QuIP#) | HF ISTA-DASLab · github.com/IST-DASLab | . | LM Studio (lmstudio-community) | Official model pool of a local inference runtime | GGUF, MLX (4/6/8-bit) | HF lmstudio-community · lmstudio.ai | . | bartowski | Well-known community publisher | GGUF, EXL2 | HF bartowski | . | unsloth | Training + quant ecosystem | 4-bit dynamic quant, GGUF | HF unsloth | . Three rules: . | The order does not change: the model owner’s official quant → hardware / inference vendor → known publisher → your own quant (same as the preference order above). | The checklist is fixed: however well-known the publisher, nothing enters production without verifying the §15 model card list. | The list ages: this is a snapshot starting list; confirm each publisher’s current activity and card transparency every time. | . Note: The same model may be published by different publishers (e.g. Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4 exists at NVIDIA, RadixArk and Inferact alike). In that case, comparing publishers must be done with the quality framework in §23. RadixArk and Inferact publish not only quants but also speculative decoding drafts (DSpark / EAGLE3).

510.title: 15. What Should a Good Model Card Disclose?
510.content: A good quantized checkpoint should give the following information as fully as possible. Not all of these carry the same weight, though; start the review with these three tiers.

511.title: Critical — the basics that must be verified
511.content: Note: What separates two quants is not the nominal bit count but the method + scaling + calibration + recipe (§6, §13). The measured summary of that difference is “a benchmark comparison against the original model” — the most valuable item on the list, and meaningless unless given with its conditions (§16). | Base model | Producer / publisher identity | Quantization method (with weight/activation precision stated) | Benchmark comparison against the original model (with its conditions: the only measurable evidence of the quality gap between two quants — §16) | .

512.title: Decisive — these settle what is left in doubt
512.content: Quantization technical details: . | Calibration dataset + algorithm + sample count (for QAT models, the training / post-training recipe and the quantization simulation instead — see §17.4) | Weight precision | Activation precision | KV cache precision (required only if the benchmark or the recommended deployment was run with a specific KV precision — it is not a checkpoint property in itself but a deployment decision: §2.2) | Mixed-precision recipe | Block / group size | . Benchmark conditions: . | Evaluation datasets | Generation settings | Context length | GPU + runtime tested | . Compatibility / scale: . | Supported GPU architectures | Tensor parallelism | .

513.title: Supporting — they do not determine technical quality, but their absence causes practical trouble
513.content: . | Quantization library + version | File integrity (commit hash / checksum) + release date | License | . The more of this information is missing, the harder it becomes to evaluate a quantized checkpoint independently.

514.title: 16. How Should a Benchmark Be Read?
514.content: When judging a quantized model’s benchmark, the score alone must not be trusted. For example: . BF16 → 88.92 NVFP4 → 88.01 . means little on its own. These must also be the same: . | benchmark version | prompt format | system prompt | temperature | top_p | max_new_tokens | context length | reasoning mode | tool configuration | . Otherwise two benchmarks cannot be compared directly. The most reliable approach is: . BF16 baseline ↓ same benchmark ↓ same generation settings ↓ same runtime ↓ quantized model ↓ same benchmark .

515.title: 17. Case Examples
515.content: The cases represent four basic scenarios, by where the quantized form originates: . | Double release — original BF16; the vendor also ships its own official FP8. | Direct low-bit release — the original model is released already quantized. | Third-party quant — the hardware / inference vendor quantizes a model released as BF16. | 4-bit through QAT — quantization enters the training stage. | . These scenarios map to the preference order in §14: 1 and 2 → the model owner’s official checkpoint, 3 → the hardware / inference vendor’s checkpoint, 4 → the model owner (production with QAT).

516.title: 17.1 Scenario 1 — Original BF16 + Official FP8: Qwen3.8-27B
516.content: Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B is a 27B-parameter model. Alongside it, Qwen also released the . Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 . checkpoint. The FP8 checkpoint uses: . | fine-grained FP8 | block size 128 | BF16 + FP8 tensor layout | . The Qwen model card states that performance metrics are close to the original model. Lesson: . Comparing the official FP8 deployment checkpoint against the BF16 baseline within the same model family is a strong start for evaluating quantization.

517.title: 17.2 Scenario 2 — Direct FP8 Release: GLM-5.3
517.content: zai-org/GLM-5.3 is a model in the 753B class and is labeled FP8 in its model repository, alongside BF16, F8_E4M3 and F32 tensor types. What matters here: . Quantization is no longer only something the community applies afterward. Model vendors can release low-precision checkpoints directly. Lesson: . The precision a model is released in becomes part of the deployment architecture.

518.title: 17.3 Scenario 3 — Third-Party Quant (NVIDIA): Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4
518.content: nvidia/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4 is a deployment checkpoint prepared with NVIDIA Model Optimizer. Its model card states these details explicitly: . | Model Optimizer v0.48.0 | mixed NVFP4/FP8 | NVFP4 → MLP + lm_head | FP8 → self-attention + linear-attention | 2.048 calibration samples | Local-Hessian calibration | Nemotron-Post-Training-Dataset-v3 | vLLM | Grace Blackwell GB300 | . The BF16 and NVFP4 results were also compared on the same benchmark set. | Benchmark | BF16 | NVFP4 | . | GPQA Diamond | 88.92 | 88.01 | . | Terminal-Bench | 75.56 | 74.02 | . | AA-LCR | 72.63 | 73.38 | . | MMMU-Pro | 75.14 | 74.86 | . | SciCode | 47.93 | 48.41 | . | IFBench | 80.07 | 78.93 | . The real lesson matters more than the individual scores: . The quantization recipe + calibration + evaluation methodology are documented openly. The checkpoint can therefore be examined and reproduced independently.

519.title: 17.4 Scenario 4 — 4-Bit with QAT: Kimi K3
519.content: moonshotai/Kimi-K3 uses: . | 2.8T total parameters | 104B activated parameters | 1M context | MXFP4 weights | MXFP8 activations | Quantization-Aware Training (from the SFT stage on) | . The inference runtimes the card suggests: vLLM, SGLang and TokenSpeed. The point that matters: . The model vendor produces the model with quantization-aware training from the SFT stage on, rather than applying quantization afterward, and releases it as MXFP4 / MXFP8. Here quantization is not a “compression step” applied after training; it is a design decision in the model’s path to release. This example changes several assumptions at once: . 1. The assumption “original = BF16, quantized = derivative” no longer holds. This model’s official release is already 4-bit. There is no “going back to BF16 to recover quality”; the reference checkpoint itself is quantized. 2. Quantization is no longer the last resort; in some models it is the only official form. This is the strongest example of the “is there an official FP8/FP4 release?” step in the §19 selection flow: the model’s produced quantized form is the model itself. 3. The subject is not only weight quantization. Taken together, MXFP4 weights + MXFP8 activations is weight+activation (full-tensor) quantization; the extreme example of the weight-only / weight+activation distinction in §6, different from AWQ/GPTQ’s weight-only approach. 4. MXFP4 is the open OCP standard. It is an example of the portability goal mentioned in §5: an open format family that does not bind you to a single vendor. Moonshot AI’s rationale is exactly this; the card states the MXFP4 / MXFP8 choice was made for “broad hardware compatibility”. 5. Quality validation is read in reverse. The question is not “how much did 4-bit lose?” but “is the 4-bit operating condition the vendor trained sufficient for my workload?” The answer comes from the model card benchmark read as in §16 and from your own production workload test. Lesson: . PTQ and QAT are not the same thing. PTQ: . BF16 model ↓ training completed ↓ quantization . QAT: . Quantized operating conditions ↓ part of the training / post-training process ↓ quantized model . Two more lessons follow: . Low bits are not always a “compromise”. In QAT, 4-bit is the target operating condition; quality is optimized for it. The “low bits = accepted loss” perception does not hold for this model class. The model card checklist (§15) reads differently for QAT models. Instead of a “calibration dataset”, look for the training/post-training recipe and the quantization simulation used in training; the calibration flow in §13 is specific to PTQ.

520.title: 18. PTQ or QAT?
520.content: | Property | PTQ | QAT | . | Can be applied after training | Yes | No / needs training | . | Cost | Lower | Higher | . | Fast for deployment | Yes | Longer process | . | Calibration needed | Usually yes | Depends on the recipe | . | Very low precision | Harder | Can be more advantageous | . | Optimizing model quality | Limited | Stronger | . | Practical for an existing model | Very suitable | More costly | . For production deployment, PTQ is the more practical starting point for most users. But for very low precision or frontier model deployment, QAT can become an important option.

521.title: 19. Quantization Selection Flow
521.content: The practical decision process should look like this: . | Define the need: required speed (TTFT / tokens/s), concurrency, context, quality threshold. | Does my hardware carry this model for this need? . | Yes → use the original model → production workload test. | No → go to step 3. | . | Choose the quantized form: . | If the model has an official FP8/FP4 release → use it. | Otherwise use a known publisher’s quant (NVIDIA, known framework / community publishers) (see §14). | If there is none → your own quant (PTQ) or a hardware / model change. | . | Does the chosen form deliver what the need asks? (speed + concurrency + quality) . | Yes → production workload test. | No → pick a model that fits your hardware and start again from step 1. | . | . Note: “Original model” = the official form the model was released in; for some models that is 4-bit from birth (see §17.4). The basic principle: . A hardware shortfall does not by itself mean “this model will not run”. The model’s quantized form may give the required speed and concurrency on the hardware you have; the goal is not to pick the lowest bits, but to meet the need at a precision the hardware is strong at. If high throughput or capacity is the target, though, lower precision may be the better economic choice.

523.title: 1. Moving to 4-bit needlessly when the hardware is enough for the original model
523.content: Lower precision is not always better. If the hardware is enough for the original model — speed, concurrency etc. — there is no reason to pay for quantization (see §19).

524.title: 2. Crediting the original model’s benchmark to the quantized model
524.content: A BF16 result: . is the result of the BF16 checkpoint. The quantized checkpoint must be verified separately.

525.title: 3. Saying “4-bit = 4-bit”
525.content: AWQ, GPTQ, NF4, MXFP4 and NVFP4 are not the same thing.

526.title: 4. Confusing native hardware acceleration with software support
526.content: A runtime accepting a format does not mean the GPU accelerates that format natively.

527.title: 5. Measuring only tokens/s
527.content: Higher throughput does not mean a better deployment. TTFT, ITL, latency and concurrency must be measured too.

528.title: 6. Forgetting the KV cache
528.content: Especially in long context, KV cache precision matters as much as weight quantization.

529.title: 7. Ignoring calibration information
529.content: Different calibration recipes of the same format can give different results.

530.title: 8. Trusting only the general benchmark
530.content: If the model’s real use is coding, test coding; if it is an agent, test agentic use; if it is RAG, test long-context retrieval performance.

531.title: 21. Summary Decision Table
531.content: | Scenario | Starting preference | . | Quality critical | BF16 / FP8 | . | Ada | Always evaluate FP8 | . | Hopper production serving | FP8 + a suitable KV cache precision | . | Ampere 4-bit | AWQ/GPTQ + optimized INT4 kernel | . | Blackwell, maximum capacity / throughput | Evaluate NVFP4 | . | Blackwell, quality first | FP8 | . | Multi-vendor deployment | MXFP4 / supported common formats | . | Long context | Weight quantization + KV cache precision together | . | Fine-tuning / QLoRA | NF4 / a suitable training precision | . | Critical production deployment | Official checkpoint + your own workload benchmark | . Note: Set up the hardware × need equation first (see §19): if your hardware carries the model for your need, use the original model; if not, look at the quantized forms.

537.title: Comparing quantizations
537.content: BF16 baseline ↓ FP8 ↓ NVFP4 / INT4 ↓ same benchmark ↓ same production workload .

538.title: 23. Evaluating Quantization Quality
538.content: No single universal threshold should be used. For example, a general rule like: . “If MMLU drops more than 1%, the quantization has failed.” . is not true. A 1% loss can be acceptable in some workloads, while in some critical coding or reasoning applications even a very small drop can matter. The more accurate approach is to weigh these together: . Quality loss × Business impact × Performance gain × Memory saving . For example, with a result like: . FP8 Quality = 100 VRAM = 100 Speed = 1.0 NVFP4 Quality = 99.2 VRAM = 55 Speed = 1.7 . NVFP4 may be the more sensible choice. But if the result is: . Quality = 95 . FP8 may be preferred for the same deployment. The right threshold therefore comes from: . the minimum quality the workload can accept + the performance required + the VRAM available .

539.title: 24. Glossary
539.content: BF16 / FP16 Generally the high-precision reference operating formats. FP8 An 8-bit floating-point format family. It has variants such as E4M3 and E5M2. NVFP4 The 4-bit floating-point format designed for NVIDIA Blackwell. It uses fine-grained scaling. MXFP4 The 4-bit floating-point format of the OCP Microscaling format family. MXFP8 The 8-bit floating-point format of the OCP Microscaling format family. It is preferred for data like activations that need higher numeric precision; for example the MXFP4 weights + MXFP8 activations combination (see §17.4). AWQ Activation-aware Weight Quantization. Common especially in weight-only INT4 deployments. GPTQ A post-training weight quantization method. EXL2 The variable bits-per-weight approach used in the ExLlama ecosystem. GGUF The model file format used in the llama.cpp ecosystem. KV cache The cache that stores the Key/Value representation of previous tokens during attention. PTQ Post-Training Quantization. Applying quantization after training is complete. QAT Quantization-Aware Training. Incorporating the effects of quantization into the model during training. Calibration The measurement process on representative data to determine the quantization parameters. Block size / group size Determines the granularity at which quantization scaling or parameter grouping is applied. Perplexity One of the fundamental metrics measuring a language model’s prediction performance. Precision The representation form that states how many bits numeric values (weights, activations, KV cache) are expressed in: “higher precision” = more bits. It is also called hassasiyet in Turkish; but it must not be confused with the model’s accuracy. Lower precision uses fewer bits; it does not automatically mean a more wrong model. MMLU / GSM8K / GPQA Benchmarks used to measure different capability areas.

540.title: 25. Conclusion
540.content: Quantization must neither be dismissed nor judged as “always faster”. In modern LLM deployment, quantization is: . a fundamental engineering tool that optimizes between memory capacity, memory bandwidth, Tensor Core throughput and deployment cost. The right choice cannot be made by looking at the bit count alone. These four questions must be asked together: . 1. At which precision was the model released? 2. Which precision does the GPU accelerate natively? 3. How was the quantization produced, with which calibration recipe? 4. What do quality and performance look like in my real workload? . Their result selects the ideal deployment: . the lowest-cost precision that meets the need, is efficiently accelerated by the GPU, and whose quality loss has been measured. So the most correct approach to quantization is: . “Pick the lowest bit count.” . No — it must be: . “Keeping the quality my workload requires, pick the precision the hardware is strong at and verify it on a real deployment.” .

Do not forget TCO in cost (the GPU cost is only 30–40% of the total). | .

545.title: 1. Introduction
545.content: LLM (Large Language Model) is an artificial intelligence model trained on very large amounts of text data that can understand and generate natural language. Most of us use these via the cloud: services like ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini run the model on their own servers, and we access it over the internet. Local LLM means running the model on your own hardware — a laptop, a desktop workstation, or a company server. Data never leaves the device, internet connectivity is not required, and there is no per-use fee. The key difference between the two approaches is: . |   | Cloud LLM | Local LLM | . | Where data is processed | On the provider’s server | On your own hardware | . | Cost model | Usage/subscription (ongoing) | Hardware (one-time) + electricity | . | Internet | Required | Not required | . | Privacy | Trust the provider | Full control | . | Model access | Limited to what the provider offers | Free choice among hundreds of open models | . | Customization | Limited | Full (fine-tuning, RAG, own data) | . The purpose of this guide is to provide a current and actionable answer to the question “Is local LLM right for me / my organization, and if so, which hardware–model–software trio should I choose?” . About Aetherix . Aetherix B.V. is a Netherlands-based provider of NVIDIA Jetson™ hardware for edge AI, specialising in Jetson platforms for robotics, automation and embedded systems. | Hardware: NVIDIA Jetson developer kits, AI kits, carrier boards and accessories; NVIDIA DGX Spark systems; NVIDIA RTX PRO graphics cards. | Expertise: a team with years of hands-on Jetson and professional GPU experience, and NVIDIA systems selected for real-world AI. | EU operations: compliant invoicing, VAT validation and transparent logistics, with European shipping from the Netherlands. | . The hardware recommendations in this guide are based on this portfolio.

546.title: 2. Why Local LLM? (Rationale)
546.content: . Figure: Key advantages of local LLM .

547.title: Advantages
547.content: Data privacy and security. This is the strongest rationale. In fields such as legal, healthcare, finance, and defense, data never leaves the device; data-protection compliance becomes significantly easier. Sensitive customer data, contracts, or patient records are not sent to a third party’s server. Data sovereignty — government and public institutions. This is one of the most decisive rationales for state agencies, critical infrastructure, and public institutions: with local LLM, corporate/classified information can never leak to overseas or third-party servers under any circumstances. Data is processed entirely within the institution’s own boundaries, on its own hardware; this directly meets data sovereignty and national security requirements. Being able to run even on completely isolated (air-gapped) and classified networks is a critical advantage for these institutions. Cost. Under intensive and continuous use, a one-time hardware investment eventually falls below the operating expense of cloud equivalents; for teams making large numbers of calls, the marginal cost in a local setup is almost only electricity. Offline operation. It works in environments without internet (the field, secure networks, air-gapped/isolated systems). Customization. You can fine-tune on your own data, bind it to your own documents with RAG, and fully control system behavior. Open-weight models do not impose the restrictions that closed services enforce. Predictable latency. Speed depends on your hardware; you are not subject to provider congestion, quota limits, or service outages.

548.title: Points to consider
548.content: . | Correct hardware matching. Your target model size requires the right VRAM/hardware class; for the most demanding workloads and the largest models, higher-memory cards or multi-GPU plans are needed (see Section 4). | Upfront investment. Hardware is a one-time investment; properly scaled, it pays for itself over the long term. | Technical knowledge. Setup, quantization choice, and driver/CUDA management require a learning curve. (New-generation tools have made this significantly easier.) | Maintenance burden. Updates, model changes, and hardware maintenance are the institution’s responsibility. | . Summary: Whenever there are privacy and data sovereignty concerns, intensive use, or a need for customization, local LLM is a strong and sustainable choice. With the right hardware–model–software match, the scale can be adjusted from small to large as needed.

549.title: 3. Who Needs It? (Target Audiences and Scenarios)
549.content: . Figure: Who needs local LLM? . Government and public institutions. Ministries, public agencies, critical infrastructure, and defense — keeping data within the country and within the institution’s own boundaries, and preventing it from leaking out, is a data sovereignty and national security requirement. For these institutions, local LLM is often the only suitable option. Enterprise (sensitive data). Law firms, hospitals/healthcare providers, finance, and defense industry — when keeping data internal is a legal/contractual obligation, local LLM is almost the only option. Developers. Unlimited prototyping without API costs; IDE integration as a code assistant; workflows with many automated tests/calls. Researchers and academics. Studying model behavior, running experiments, fine-tuning studies, and scientific work that requires full control over the model. SMEs. Small and medium-sized businesses that want to build customer service, document processing, and internal automation without exposing customer data. Individual/privacy-focused users. Personal assistant, note/email management, hobby use; those who do not want to give their data to any company. Those for whom keeping scale small is enough: For occasional and light use only, an entry-level card or an existing workstation is often sufficient; as needs grow, the hardware can scale gradually (see Section 4).

551.title: 4.1. Why NVIDIA? In one word: CUDA
551.content: The main reason to choose NVIDIA for local LLM hardware is CUDA. CUDA is the software platform NVIDIA offers for parallel computing on GPUs, and it has become the de facto standard of the AI world. Its practical consequences are: . | Ecosystem compatibility. Nearly all LLM tools and libraries — PyTorch, TensorFlow, vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, llama.cpp, Ollama — are developed primarily on CUDA and run best on NVIDIA hardware. Newly released models, quantization formats, and optimizations are published for CUDA first. | Maturity and prevalence. CUDA has been under development for over a decade; it provides extensive documentation, community support, and an abundance of ready-made solutions. When you encounter a problem, the solution most likely already exists. | Seamless setup. A “works out of the box” experience; the risk of driver, library, and toolchain incompatibility is minimized. | . For this reason, throughout this guide only NVIDIA is covered on the hardware side; alternative platforms have not yet reached this level of maturity and ecosystem breadth. While in classic IT, CPU + RAM + storage is often sufficient, in LLMs GPU choice directly determines whether the model can run at all: VRAM determines the model size that can be run, memory bandwidth determines the token generation rate, and FLOPS determines training/inference speed. Wrong GPU = the model either does not run at all or runs very slowly.

552.title: 4.2. First decision: Training or Inference?
552.content: This is the most important question that determines hardware requirements. The answer to “Will training be done?” defines the scale of hardware you will need from the start. Figure: First decision: training or inference? . For most organizations, the starting point is inference — running a ready open model on your own server. Training/customization comes into play only when the model needs to be adapted to your own data, and it has four tiers: . |   | Pre-training (from scratch) | Full Fine-tune | Fine-tune (LoRA) | Fine-tune (QLoRA) | Inference | . | VRAM requirement | Very high (~16× params) | High (~12–14× params) | Medium (~2–3× params) | Low (~0.6–1× params) | Model + KV cache | . | 7B model | 8× B200 (1 team) | 1× H200 (~85–100 GB) | 1× L40S / RTX PRO 6000 | 1× L40S | 1× L40S / RTX PRO 6000 | . | 70B model | 8–16× B300 (1–2 teams) | 4–8× H200 (ZeRO-3) | 2–4× H200 | 1× DGX Spark / 1× H200 | 1× H200 (INT8) / 1× DGX Spark (INT8) — for FP16, 2× H200 (see 4.8) | . | Duration | Weeks–months | Days–1 week | Hours | Hours | — | . | Data requirement | Trillions of tokens | Millions of examples | Thousands of examples | Thousands of examples | — | . | Cost | Very high | High | Medium | Low | Medium | . | Pre-training (from scratch): The heaviest scenario; only for institutions training their own base model. Requires a B200/B300 cluster. Note: The “8×/16×” figures in the table are not the actual compute requirement but the minimum sales unit of B200/B300 (an 8-GPU team — see 4.5/D). The actual VRAM requirement is roughly 16× the model size (FP16 weights + gradients + Adam optimizer states): 7B full training ≈ 120–150 GB, 70B ≈ 1 TB+ (plus activations). So 7B full training needs far less memory than a single 8-GPU team; even if the whole team is not used, this is the smallest sales unit. | Full Fine-tune: Updates all parameters of a pre-trained model on your own data. VRAM requirement is close to pre-training (~12–14× params — slightly lower thanks to gradient checkpointing and typically shorter sequences), but duration and data are far less. Suited for deep domain adaptation (specialized fields such as Turkish, medical, legal); comes into play when LoRA is insufficient. Risk — catastrophic forgetting: Updating all parameters can degrade or overwrite the general capabilities learned during pre-training (other languages, general knowledge, reasoning). LoRA/QLoRA largely mitigates this risk — base model weights are kept frozen and only small adapter layers are trained; domain adaptation is added while general capabilities are preserved. In practice, most organizations should start with LoRA/QLoRA. When full fine-tuning is chosen, mitigate the risk with: a low learning rate, data mixing (domain data + general data together), regularization (KL/L2), and limiting the number of epochs. (Open-source tools: see 6.F.) | LoRA / QLoRA fine-tune: The practical way to adapt an existing model to your own data. It does not train the whole model, only small additional layers. Memory accounting: In LoRA, base weights are frozen, so only FP16 weights (~2× params) + gradient-checkpointed activations + small adapter gradients/Adam states contribute → ~2–3× params; in QLoRA, base weights are quantized to 4-bit NF4 (~0.5× params), plus activations and small adapter overhead → ~0.6–1× params. Fine-tuning a 70B model even with a single DGX Spark is possible (with QLoRA — in FP16-based LoRA, the 70B weights alone are ~140 GB, so they do not fit in 128 GB). (Open-source tools: see 6.F.) | Inference: Just running the model. Here, the extra VRAM allocated for KV cache is critical (see 4.3); as the number of concurrent users grows, this load grows. | .

553.title: 4.3. The decisive metric: VRAM (and total memory budget)
553.content: In local LLM, the single hard constraint is VRAM (graphics card memory). If the model weights + KV cache do not fit in GPU memory, it either spills to system RAM (~10x slowdown) or the model does not run at all. Rule of thumb (weights only): . | FP16 (16-bit): ~2 GB VRAM / billion parameters | 8-bit (Q8): half of that (~1 GB / billion) | 4-bit (Q4, e.g. Q4_K_M): a quarter (~0.5 GB / billion). Q4_K_M is considered the optimal quality/memory balance because it retains ~92–95% of full precision while reducing memory ~4×. | . Approximate VRAM by model size (weights; add KV cache + headroom on top): . | Model | FP16 | 8-bit | 4-bit (Q4_K_M) | . | 7B / 8B | ~14–16 GB | ~8 GB | ~5 GB | . | 14B | ~28 GB | ~15 GB | ~9–10 GB | . | 32B | ~64 GB | ~34 GB | ~18–20 GB | . | 70B | ~140 GB | ~70 GB | ~38–48 GB | . KV cache / context length impact (often overlooked). KV cache grows linearly with context length and the number of concurrent requests; for long contexts it can exceed even the model weights. Example: Llama 3.1 70B, a single request with 128K context, can alone consume ~40 GB of KV cache — and this value already assumes the model uses GQA (Grouped-Query Attention); a classic (MHA) architecture without GQA would require ~8× more for the same scenario. Mitigation: quantizing the KV cache to FP8/INT8 roughly halves the memory. Total VRAM budget. The real requirement is not just the weights: . Total VRAM = Model Weights + KV Cache + Activations + Overhead . | Component | Calculation | Example | . | Model weights | parameters × bytes/param | 7B FP16 = 14 GB · 70B FP16 = 140 GB | . | Max context (max_len) | directly determines KV cache size | 4K → 128K tokens = ~32× KV cache difference | . | KV cache | 2 × layers × kv_heads × head_dim × max_len × batch × 2 bytes | 70B (GQA, 8 KV head), 4096 tokens, batch 32 ≈ 20–40 GB | . | Activations | batch × max_len × hidden_dim × layers | Large in training, small in inference | . | Overhead | ~10–20% extra | Fragmentation, temporary buffers | . Formula note: In GQA models, kv_heads is a small fraction of the total attention head count (e.g. Llama 3.1 70B: 64 heads → 8 KV head); the 20–40 GB example in the table is therefore low. In a classic (MHA) architecture without GQA, kv_heads = number of heads, and the same scenario requires ~8× more memory. Rule: Always leave ~20% extra VRAM headroom. To simplify the calculation, you can use the free tool Cordatus VRAM Calculator — https://app.cordatus.ai/#/vram-calculator .

554.title: 4.4. How inference works and quality-of-service metrics
554.content: Two-stage inference — why are there two separate bottlenecks? An LLM request is processed in two stages: . | Prefill (prompt processing): All tokens in the input prompt are processed at once (in parallel); heavy matrix multiplications dominate → compute-bound (FLOPS-dependent). This stage determines TTFT — a long prompt = long TTFT. | Decode (token generation): The response is generated token by token, sequentially; since each token depends on the previous one (autoregressive), it cannot be parallelized within a single request. At each step, all model weights are re-read from memory, but the compute is relatively small → memory-bound (memory-bandwidth-dependent). This stage determines TPS. Generation continues until an EOS (end-of-sequence) token is produced or the maximum token limit is reached. | . This is why two different hardware properties matter: FLOPS for prefill/TTFT and memory bandwidth for decode/TPS. Although decode does not parallelize within a single request, batching distributes weight reads across many requests, increasing total throughput. Hardware selection is shaped not only by “does the model fit” but also by “what user experience are we targeting.” Four key metrics: . | TTFT (Time to First Token): How long after the user submits the prompt does the first token arrive? Compute-bound — depends on FLOPS. | TPS (Tokens Per Second): How many tokens are generated per second? Directly affects user experience. Memory-bound — depends on memory bandwidth. | Throughput: How many requests are processed per unit time? Increases as batch grows. | Batch size — the fundamental trade-off: High batch → high throughput but high latency; low batch → low latency but low throughput. Finding the optimal point is critical. | . Practical takeaway: if you want fast single-user responses, high bandwidth (TPS) and FLOPS (TTFT) matter; if you want multi-user high throughput, you need to scale the batch and therefore VRAM (KV cache). Techniques that accelerate the system (2026). Various software-layer methods exist to speed up these two stages; most are supported by vLLM / SGLang / TensorRT-LLM and generally kick in without changing the model: . | Speculative decoding: A small “draft” model proposes multiple tokens, and the large model verifies them in a single pass → 2–3× speedup in decode. The current strongest approach is EAGLE-3 / EAGLE 3.1 (a lightweight prediction head attached to the model’s inner layers, which does not require a separate draft model) and its parallel variant P-EAGLE. | MTP (Multi-Token Prediction): The model predicts multiple tokens in a single step (e.g. DeepSeek architecture); used as a draft both in training and speculative decoding. | Disaggregated prefill (prefill/decode separation): Distributes compute-bound prefill and memory-bound decode across separate GPU pools; each stage scales according to its own bottleneck, improving latency and throughput together (e.g. NVIDIA Dynamo). | Continuous / in-flight batching: Dynamically adds and removes requests from the batch, keeping the GPU busy → high throughput. | Chunked prefill & prefix caching: Splits long prefill and interleaves it with decode to lower TTFT; KV cache is reused for common prefixes (system prompt) (PagedAttention / RadixAttention — see 6.A). | KV cache quantization (FP8/INT8): Reduces the memory load of decode (see 4.3). | . With the right inference engine and configuration, these techniques can produce a 2–4× speed/throughput difference in production setups — software configuration matters as much as hardware.

556.title: 4.6. Multi-GPU
556.content: When a single card’s VRAM is insufficient for the target model, multiple cards are pooled (e.g. 2× RTX PRO 5000 = 96 GB, or 2× RTX PRO 6000 = 192 GB). The rationale: running 70B+ and large MoE models with high precision / long context. Professional/data center cards are designed for multi-GPU scaling; the workload is distributed via tensor parallelism (each layer is split across cards, requires high bandwidth) or pipeline parallelism (layers are distributed across cards, light inter-card traffic). vLLM and TensorRT-LLM support both. In multi-node setups, InfiniBand/Ethernet bandwidth and PCIe bottlenecks must not be overlooked.

557.title: 4.7. CPU + RAM only
557.content: Suitable for entry, small/quantized models, and batch/non-interactive work (e.g. document summarization); not for fluid chat. The bottleneck is not compute but memory bandwidth. A typical 8-core desktop CPU achieves ~5–15 tok/s on a 7B model; large models drop to single digits. A model that fits in VRAM is roughly ~10× faster than one spilled to RAM. llama.cpp can keep some layers on the GPU and offload the rest to RAM — good as a short-term solution, not for production speed.

560.title: 5. Model Selection
560.content: . Figure: Model selection by task . Size–cost balance: for most local workloads, 7–14B dense or ~30B MoE (~3B active) models are the optimal balance; the most demanding tasks require 70B+ / large MoE.

561.title: 5.1. What can you do with a local LLM? (inference use cases)
561.content: Before selecting a model, “what task will I do?” must be clear — the task determines both the model and the hardware. For most organizations, the starting point is inference, not training (see 4.2) and RAG is only one of these. It is practical to group the use cases into two: . Interactive (low latency matters — TPS/TTFT decisive): . | Chat / assistant — general Q&A, enterprise/personal assistant | RAG / document Q&A — with your own documents (only one of these) | Code assistance — IDE assistant, code generation/explanation/review, test generation | Agent & automation (agentic) — tool calling, email triage, calendar, multi-step workflows | Translation — translating classified documents locally without exposing them | . Batch / non-interactive (batch — latency irrelevant; small/cheap hardware suffices, see 4.7): . | Summarization — meetings, contracts, long reports, email piles | Information extraction — invoice/contract/form → structured JSON, NER | Classification / routing — request triage, sentiment analysis, content moderation, PII detection | Semantic search / recommendation / clustering — with embedding models | Synthetic / labeled data generation — data preparation for fine-tuning | Multimodal — OCR’d document analysis, visual Q&A, audio transcription + LLM | Guardrail / auditing — auditing another model’s output, PII masking | . Practical takeaway: Because batch jobs are latency-insensitive, they reduce hardware requirements — the same organization can run archive summarization on a small card and live chat on a large card. Your task profile jointly determines the hardware class in §4 and the model choice below.

562.title: 5.2. Model selection criteria
562.content: The right model is not “the one with the highest benchmark score” but the one best suited to your task + hardware + constraints. Weigh the criteria below by your task priorities: . | Criterion | Question to ask | . | Task fit | Chat, code, reasoning, or extraction? | . | Size / VRAM budget | Does it fit the hardware? In MoE, total parameters determine memory (all experts are loaded into VRAM); active parameters determine only speed | . | Context length | How many tokens needed? (Determines KV cache load — see 4.3) | . | Turkish / language performance | Not the general score, but Turkish benchmarks (see 5.6) | . | License | Is commercial use allowed? (see 5.7) | . | Architecture | Dense vs MoE — speed/memory trade-off | . | Quantizability | Is Q4/AWQ quality loss acceptable? Are GGUF/AWQ available? | . | Tool-calling / JSON reliability | Critical for agents & structured output (small models struggle) | . | Multimodality | Are vision/audio needed? | . | Fine-tunability | Is the base model + ecosystem (Unsloth/Axolotl) available? | . | Ecosystem / maintenance | Are ready quants, variants, and active development available? | . Criteria are weighted by task: in a code assistant, tool-calling + SWE-bench stand out; in government/legal document processing, Turkish performance + license + citation accuracy are decisive. Validate the choice with your own usage, not a single “leader model” (see 5.9).

563.title: 5.3. Current open-weight model families (mid-2026)
563.content: Note: In 2026, momentum has clearly shifted to Chinese open-weight labs (Qwen, DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, MiniMax). Most new models use the MoE (Mixture-of-Experts) architecture: total parameters are large, but only a small “active” portion runs at each step → large-model quality at small-model operating cost. | Qwen (Alibaba) — the most active family. Qwen3-235B-A22B (235B total / 22B active, Apache 2.0). In February 2026, the Qwen3.5 series (flagship Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, ~1M context; plus 0.8B–27B dense and 35B-A3B / 122B-A10B MoE variants). The newer Qwen3.6-35B-A3B rivals the older 397B in coding. 100–200+ languages. | DeepSeek — In April 2026, DeepSeek V4 (MIT): V4-Pro (1.6T / 49B active, 1M context) and V4-Flash (284B / 13B active). The older R1 reasoning model and distilled versions (1.5B–70B) remain very common. | Llama (Meta) — the Llama 4 family: Scout (109B/17B active, 10M context), Maverick (~400B/17B active, 1M context). The largest “Behemoth” appears to have been practically shelved (not officially confirmed). License is restrictive (see 5.7). | Google Gemma — Gemma 4: E2B (phone), E4B (edge), 12B, 26B-A4B (MoE), 31B dense. 140+ languages, multimodal (text+image) from 4B onward. | Mistral — Mistral Large 3 (675B/41B active, multimodal) and Mistral Small 4 (Apache 2.0). The 24B Magistral reasoning model. | Microsoft Phi — Phi-4 family (~14B reasoning models, MIT). Strong in reasoning per parameter, ideal for local. | 2026 risers: GLM-5.1 (Zhipu/Z.ai) (~744B/40B active, MIT, strong agent/coding), Kimi K2.6 (Moonshot) (~1T/32B active, multimodal, among the best open models in coding), MiniMax M3 (June 2026; frontier coding + 1M context + multimodality together), MiMo V2.5 Pro (Xiaomi) (at the top of open-weight intelligence). NVIDIA’s open model Nemotron 3 and Gemma 4 are the strongest non-Chinese open options; OpenAI’s open-weight gpt-oss series also runs locally. | .

564.title: 5.4. Parameter size ↔ performance balance
564.content: . | Small (1–4B): In 2026, genuinely useful — autocomplete, summarization, smart replies, simple Q&A, light code help. Runs on phones and 6 GB VRAM. | 7–14B dense or ~30B MoE (~3B active): The optimal balance for most local workloads — chat, RAG, code assistance, agent tasks. MoEs like Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Gemma 4 26B-A4B deliver near-large-model quality at small-model cost. | 70B+ / large MoE: For the hardest reasoning, complex multi-step agent-coding, very long context, and the highest benchmark scores. Requires multi-GPU / serious VRAM. | .

565.title: 5.5. Quantization
565.content: . | Formats: GGUF (llama.cpp/Ollama/LM Studio; CPU+GPU; most common locally), GPTQ (GPU), AWQ (activation-aware, slightly better than GPTQ at 4-bit). | Quality/bit: FP16 = full quality · 8-bit ≈ near-lossless · Q4_K_M ≈ ~92–95% of quality · AWQ 4-bit ≈ ~95%. At 4-bit, the loss is ~1–2% for most tasks. | 2026 developments: imatrix (importance-matrix) quants improve quality at the same bit; Unsloth Dynamic 2.0 sets bits per layer; hardware-native MXFP4 for Blackwell; FP8 is common in server setups. | .

566.title: 5.6. Selection by task (including Turkish)
566.content: . | General chat: Qwen3/3.5 (multilingual, Apache 2.0), Gemma 4 (multimodal, edge-friendly). | Coding/agent: Kimi K2.6, GLM-5.1, DeepSeek V4-Pro, MiniMax M3, Qwen3.6 (Qwen-Coder). | Top-tier general intelligence (including reasoning): In 2026, reasoning is not a separate category. The Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (v4.0; combines agent + coding + scientific reasoning + general capability, https://artificialanalysis.ai) shows that the same models lead in intelligence, coding, and reasoning at the open-weight top. Current open-weight leaders: Kimi K2.6, DeepSeek V4-Pro, GLM-5.1 (all three statistically tied), followed by MiMo V2.5 Pro (Xiaomi) and Qwen3.6. The strongest non-Chinese open models: Google Gemma 4 and NVIDIA Nemotron 3. (Note: Qwen3.7 Max/Plus are closed API models, not open-weight.) For compact/local reasoning, Phi-4 and Magistral 24B are strong per parameter. | Turkish / multilingual: The best general multilingual open models are Qwen3/3.5 (200+ languages) and Gemma 3/4 (140+ languages). On TurkBench, Qwen3-235B-Inst scored 73.4 and Gemma-3-12B-TR 71.4 (large models consistently lead). Turkish-specific models: ytu-ce-cosmos Turkish-Llama-8b (YTÜ, Llama-3-based), Trendyol-LLM v4.1.0 (Qwen2.5-7B + 13B on Turkish tokens), CosmosGPT (355M–774M, Turkish-only), MODA (Qwen2.5-7B continued pre-training, 2026). Turkish benchmarks: TurkishMMLU, Cetvel, TurkBench. | Embedding & reranking models for RAG: RAG quality depends on the embedding model as much as on the LLM — if the wrong chunk is retrieved, even the best model cannot answer correctly. Strong open options for multilingual/Turkish: BGE-M3, multilingual-e5, Jina embeddings v3, Nomic Embed; for reranking, the bge-reranker class. Embeddings also run locally (e.g. TEI); for Turkish-heavy work, choose multilingual/Turkish versions and validate on your own documents (see 5.9). | .
