The accuracy here is therefore not comparable with TDB accuracy. | Model | accuracy | noul | choice | score | score-MAE (norm) | mean gold p | p50/p95 ms | . | clef | 0.855 | 0.950 | 0.895 | 0.718 | 0.120 | 0.788 | 488 / 2221 | . | d3-27b | 0.840 | 0.975 | 0.850 | 0.692 | 0.114 | 0.810 | 451 / 2547 | . | d3-mini | 0.832 | 0.975 | 0.900 | 0.615 | 0.142 | 0.749 | 78 / 388 | . | clef-flash | 0.786 | 0.875 | 0.921 | 0.564 | 0.168 | 0.728 | 148 / 810 | . | d1-3b | 0.624 | 0.800 | 0.605 | 0.462 | 0.220 | 0.560 | 88 / 201 | . | d3-edge | 0.429 | 0.500 | 0.450 | 0.333 | 0.311 | 0.370 | 15 / 52 | . score questions are the type every model struggles with most. In long and complex Turkish corporate texts the model tends to drift between adjacent levels: the distinction between “medium” and “medium-high” cannot be made reliably. Although clef achieves the highest accuracy at 0.718, this does not mean that an ordered scale can be used automatically in production.

682.doc: System One in Production: Decision Quality, Reliability and Performance on DGX Spark with vLLM and SGLang
682.title: 4. Confidence and uncertainty

683.doc: System One in Production: Decision Quality, Reliability and Performance on DGX Spark with vLLM and SGLang
683.title: 4.1. What confidence does not say
683.content: confidence expresses the probability the model reports for the answer it chose; it does not directly indicate the probability that the answer is actually correct. A high confidence report therefore does not mean the decision is necessarily right. In the 42 ambiguity controls in TDB, the 27B models selected one of the valid options in 95–98% of cases; the highest average probability of the selected options was in the 0.75–0.77 range. In other words, the models tend to settle on one of the options rather than abstain, and they do so with relatively high probability. The level of uncertainty is not represented directly by a separate field in the API output. label_mass partly fills this gap, but only in the D1 family. In D3 and CLEF the value is fixed at 1.0; label_mass therefore cannot be used as a safety filter on its own in these families. The practical consequence: a confidence threshold is necessary but not sufficient; it must be calibrated on labelled data.

684.doc: System One in Production: Decision Quality, Reliability and Performance on DGX Spark with vLLM and SGLang
684.title: 4.2. Coverage–risk analysis
684.content: The boundary between automatic decision and human review is set not by overall accuracy but by the error rate among decisions given with high confidence. The table below is computed on the 354 scored cases of TDB by varying the confidence threshold. | Model | conf ≥ 0.8 | conf ≥ 0.9 | conf ≥ 0.95 | . | d3-27b | Coverage 0.92 · risk 0.021 | Coverage 0.87 · risk 0.013 | Coverage 0.80 · risk 0.011 | . | clef | Coverage 0.85 · risk 0.023 | Coverage 0.69 · risk 0.008 | Coverage 0.48 · risk 0.006 | . | clef-flash | Coverage 0.68 · risk 0.046 | Coverage 0.49 · risk 0.023 | Coverage 0.25 · risk 0.000 | . | d3-mini | Coverage 0.68 · risk 0.021 | Coverage 0.56 · risk 0.010 | Coverage 0.43 · risk 0.007 | . | d1-3b | Coverage 0.22 · risk 0.195 | Coverage 0.12 · risk 0.122 | Coverage 0.03 · risk 0.000 | . | d3-edge | Coverage 0.25 · risk 0.596 | Coverage 0.12 · risk 0.523 | Coverage 0.07 · risk 0.360 | . Coverage: the share of decisions meeting the confidence threshold among all decisions. Risk: the error rate among decisions resolved automatically. The most important distinction in the table is between d3-27b and clef. At the 0.90 threshold d3-27b closes 87% of cases with 1.3% risk, while clef closes 69% with 0.8% risk. Lower risk comes at the price of more human review; the choice depends on the cost of a wrong decision. For d3-edge, confidence is not a reliable indicator: even when the model reports high confidence, the error rate remains in the 0.36–0.60 range. d1-3b similarly shows high risk at low coverage. These results apply only to the dataset and test conditions used. If the distribution of production data changes, the same coverage and risk levels cannot be guaranteed. The thresholds must therefore be recalibrated on the application’s own labelled data.

685.doc: System One in Production: Decision Quality, Reliability and Performance on DGX Spark with vLLM and SGLang
685.title: 5. Multimodal input, boundary cases, performance

686.doc: System One in Production: Decision Quality, Reliability and Performance on DGX Spark with vLLM and SGLang
686.title: 5.1. Image and video
686.content: Images and video can be added to the state field. In D3 and CLEF, images are processed at up to 1.6 megapixels and video at 2 frames per second and at most 32 frames. D1 supports only images and downsamples them to 1024×1024. | Model | Correct answers | Note | . | d3-27b | 8/8 | The only model to answer every item correctly | . | d3-mini | 7/8 | — | . | clef | 7/8 | — | . | d1-3b | 6/7 | Video not supported; g7 was not run, requests containing videos returned an error | . | clef-flash | 6/8 | — | . | d3-edge | 6/8 | — | . The common weakness is the item coded g3: reading a numeric value from a chart. Every model except d3-27b answered this question incorrectly and produced different values in the 0.7–1.9 range. The models can determine the overall trend of the chart but struggle to read exact numeric values. In workflows where numerical accuracy is critical, the model output must therefore be verified against a data source independent of the image. In the D3 family, media is processed once and the resulting representation is shared across all questions. In the tests, asking 16 questions in a single request and in 16 separate requests gave the same result; in image-heavy workloads this reduces cost by avoiding repeated processing.

687.doc: System One in Production: Decision Quality, Reliability and Performance on DGX Spark with vLLM and SGLang
687.title: 5.2. Concurrent request performance
687.content: | Model | 1 client | 8 clients | . | d3-edge | 118.6 | 335.6 | . | d1-3b | 21.0 | 107.2 | . | d3-mini | 19.0 | 39.2 | . | clef-flash | 8.8 | 16.8 | . | d3-27b | 2.5 | 5.9 | . | clef | 3.1 | 4.9 | . Values are completed requests per second (req/s), measured with single-question requests; for latency see the p50/p95 columns in §3. At a single request, latency depends largely on the duration of one forward pass. Because D3 evaluates each question in a separate pass while CLEF can evaluate several questions in a single forward pass, CLEF’s latency advantage grows as the number of questions increases.

688.doc: System One in Production: Decision Quality, Reliability and Performance on DGX Spark with vLLM and SGLang
688.title: 6. Engine portability: vLLM and SGLang
688.content: For a system not to depend on a single inference engine, it must be known whether the same API produces the same decision. The same client scripts, the same datasets and the same model roster were run on both engines. This section measures agreement between two engines with pinned versions; it makes no claim about the general behaviour of the engines. V: vLLM, S: SGLang. | Model | TDB (V→S) | cisimcik (V→S) | std72 (V→S) | tr-set (V→S) | vision-8 (V→S) | Portability | . | d3-27b | 0.963 → 0.966 | 0.840 → 0.840 | 1.000 → 1.000 | 0.943 → 0.943 | 1.000 → 1.000 | Yes (protected mode) | . | clef | 0.9435 → 0.9435 | 0.855 → 0.856 | 1.000 → 0.972 | — → 0.914* | 0.875 → 0.875 | Yes | . | clef-flash | 0.853 → 0.853 | 0.786 → 0.782 | 0.972 → 0.972 | — → 0.857* | 0.750 → 0.875 | Yes | . | d1-3b | 0.545 → 0.568 | 0.624 → 0.622 | 0.931 → 0.931 | — → 0.829* | 0.857 → 0.875 | Yes | . | d3-mini | 0.887 → 0.280 ⚠ | 0.832 → 0.319 ⚠ | 1.000 → 0.292 ⚠ | 0.886 → 0.257 ⚠ | 0.875 → 0.250 ⚠ | No | . | d3-edge | 0.336 → ✗ | — → ✗ | 0.819 → ✗ | 0.800 → ✗ | 0.750 → ✗ | No | . * tr-set was run only on SGLang; there is no vLLM counterpart in these rows. ✗: the model could not be started in SGLang.

689.doc: System One in Production: Decision Quality, Reliability and Performance on DGX Spark with vLLM and SGLang
689.title: 6.1. Differences at the API level
689.content: That the same client code produces the same result on both engines in the D1 and CLEF families shows that the observed differences do not come from the client. There are, however, mismatches at the schema level, and the client must handle each of them separately. | The model field is mandatory in SGLang. When it is omitted, 422 Field required is returned; in vLLM it is optional. A compatible client must obtain the model name from /v1/models and add it to the body. | confidence may not match the probability of the selected option. In the SGLang output the example choice: "diger", confidence: 0.303, probabilities: {…, "diger": 0.536} was observed. According to the schema these two values should be equal. In SGLang, confidence must not be used in threshold calculations without verification. | probabilities is absent in noul answers. While vLLM returns a {yes, no} distribution, SGLang gives only {"type":"noul","noul":0.117}. The missing probability can be derived with P(no) = 1 − P(yes) because noul is binary. | The location of label_mass differs. vLLM returns it under diagnostics[qid].{label_mass, argmax_is_label}, while SGLang returns it in the per-answer x_label_mass field; moreover, the field is absent in the d3-mini output. A missing value must not be silently accepted as valid. | Error codes differ. An unknown question field returns 400 in vLLM and 422 in SGLang; chat_template_kwargs is ignored with 200 in vLLM but returns 400 in SGLang. Options with the same name after truncation are accepted in both engines; the option, question and level limits are the same. | .

690.doc: System One in Production: Decision Quality, Reliability and Performance on DGX Spark with vLLM and SGLang
690.title: 6.2. Speed
690.content: | Model | SGLang req/s (1 / 8) | Relative to vLLM | . | d1-3b | 27 / 63 | About 1/4 of vLLM under high load | . | d3-mini | 17 / 37 | Similar; falls at 64 clients | . | clef-flash | 8 / 15 | On a par | . | d3-27b | 3 / 7 | Slightly higher in protected mode | . | clef | 3 / 5 | Equal | . The vLLM values are given in §5.2.

691.doc: System One in Production: Decision Quality, Reliability and Performance on DGX Spark with vLLM and SGLang
691.title: 6.3. Conclusion
691.content: The results in this section are compatibility observations obtained only for the versions tested; they must not be interpreted as a general portability rule. In the versions tested, the label-token method (D1) and the joint-schema method (CLEF) produced similar results on both engines; the 27B D3 model is compatible in protected mode. The degradation seen in the small D3 models does not mean that the engine does not support this method in general. What it shows is that the answer-code implementation in that development image produced incorrect results on small models. Because the failure was observed in one model and one version, no firm judgement can be made about its cause; numerical precision, the attention path and schema mapping must each be examined separately. Every model–engine–version combination must therefore pass a separate verification test before production, and the test must be repeated when the engine version is upgraded. In terms of performance, SGLang may provide slightly lower latency at a single request, while vLLM’s batching advantage becomes evident under high concurrency on d1-3B.

692.doc: System One in Production: Decision Quality, Reliability and Performance on DGX Spark with vLLM and SGLang
692.title: 7. Decision guide for production

693.doc: System One in Production: Decision Quality, Reliability and Performance on DGX Spark with vLLM and SGLang
693.title: 7.1. Model selection
693.content: | Option | When | Limitation | . | d3-27b (27B) | When accuracy is critical; when there are complex inputs including image and video | ~340 ms single-request latency | . | clef (27B) | When the single-forward-pass advantage is needed for multi-question requests | ~98% of d3-27b accuracy | . | clef-flash (9B) | 2–9 questions per request; when the cost of a wrong decision is low | TDB 0.853 | . | d3-mini (4B) | Real-time pre-filtering; ~50 ms budget | TDB score 0.615; unusable in the SGLang image tested | . | d1-3b (3B) | High-volume labelling; ~60 ms budget | TDB 0.545; LFM 1.0 licence | . | d3-edge (0.6B) | First routing only; when the cost of error is very low | TDB 0.336; confidence threshold meaningless | . The relationship between size and accuracy is not uniform: clef (27B) and d3-27b (27B) have similar accuracy, while d3-mini (4B) is better than the 9B clef-flash on TDB. The choice depends on the readout method and the task rather than on the parameter count.

694.doc: System One in Production: Decision Quality, Reliability and Performance on DGX Spark with vLLM and SGLang
694.title: 7.2. Recommended decision policy
694.content: . | Threshold: As an initial policy, confidence ≥ 0.90 and label_mass ≥ 0.95 are required together. For d3-27b this resolves about 87% of 354 cases automatically with 1.3% risk. The thresholds are verified with the application data before going to production. | Routing to human review: When label_mass < 0.95, the decision goes to human review. In D3 and CLEF this field is fixed at 1.0, so it is not sufficient on its own; task categories with high error rates (by_category) and Turkish score questions are also routed. | Record keeping: confidence and, where possible, the probability distribution are stored with each decision; the thresholds are updated in line with new results and the coverage–risk analysis is repeated with real data. | Re-querying: In batched runs and runs that depend on memory state, probabilities may vary by about ±0.07. Decisions close to the threshold are verified with a single request before publication; where possible, a configuration that provides deterministic behaviour (VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT) is evaluated. | What to avoid: Basing a production decision on d3-edge alone; treating confidence as calibrated accuracy; embedding d1-3B in an Apache-2.0-compatible product without examining the licence terms. | .

695.doc: System One in Production: Decision Quality, Reliability and Performance on DGX Spark with vLLM and SGLang
695.title: 8. Risks, licences and conclusion

696.doc: System One in Production: Decision Quality, Reliability and Performance on DGX Spark with vLLM and SGLang
696.title: 8.1. Limits of validity
696.content: . | The results apply to a single hardware configuration (DGX Spark GB10), a single memory configuration and the development images of two engines. | The TDB and cisimcik labels were not changed within the scope of this study; the results must be reproduced when new versions are published. | The 27B results were obtained with the protected protocol (GPU memory utilization 0.78, --enforce-eager, batched runs); latency and stability may change under different settings. | For tr-set, clef, clef-flash and d1-3b were measured only on SGLang; cross-engine comparison cannot be made for these three models. | Zero-byte result files were not counted as complete, and missing tests were rerun with FORCE=1. | Use of the TypeSafe SDK with the two engines is not included in this scope. | .

697.doc: System One in Production: Decision Quality, Reliability and Performance on DGX Spark with vLLM and SGLang
697.title: 8.2. Licences
697.content: Status verified against Hugging Face model cards and repository files as of November 2026: . | Model | Licence | Base model | . | vllm-sr/d3 | Apache-2.0 | Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B (Apache-2.0) | . | vllm-sr/d3-mini | Apache-2.0 | Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B (Apache-2.0) | . | vllm-sr/d3-edge | Apache-2.0 | Qwen/Qwen3.5-0.8B (Apache-2.0) | . | Cloudflare/clef | Apache-2.0 | Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B | . | Cloudflare/clef-flash | Apache-2.0 | Qwen3.5 (9B) | . | LiquidAI/d1-3B | LFM 1.0 ⚠ | LiquidAI/LFM2.5-VL-3B | . The D3 and CLEF families are published under Apache-2.0; nevertheless, when redistribution and derivative work are evaluated, the licence file of the version used, and any additional terms, should be examined in addition to the model card. d1-3B is not Apache-2.0. The rights that apply in Apache-2.0-licensed software must not be assumed to apply unchanged; before commercial distribution or inclusion in a product, Liquid AI’s current licence text should be examined and, if necessary, legal advice obtained.

698.doc: System One in Production: Decision Quality, Reliability and Performance on DGX Spark with vLLM and SGLang
698.title: 8.3. Conclusion
698.content: This evaluation shows that the System One family can be used in production under certain conditions, but that a reliable deployment requires the model, inference engine and hardware combination to be verified together. | Accuracy increases with size, but 4B-class models come much closer to 27B than expected; the choice should be made by task and readout method, not by parameter count. | Confidence is not calibrated; uncertainty is not represented in the output. Automatic decisions must be built with thresholds validated on labelled data and with human review. | Turkish: the weakest points are ordered score questions and paraphrase consistency; both must be tested separately with institution-specific data. | Engine agreement depends on the model and the engine version: D1 and CLEF are portable in the versions tested, 27B D3 is portable in protected mode, and the small D3 models do not work in the SGLang image tested. | Hardware is a real limit: 27B models cannot be run reliably on GB10 without a protected operating protocol. | . The decision to go to production should rest on thresholds verified on application-specific labelled data, continuous monitoring of decision records, and separate acceptance tests run for every model–engine–version combination.

699.doc: System One in Production: Decision Quality, Reliability and Performance on DGX Spark with vLLM and SGLang
699.title: System One in Production: Decision Quality, Reliability and Performance on DGX Spark with vLLM and SGLang
699.content: Prepared by: Aetherix B.V. — Trusted Jetson Hardware Provider for Edge AI . Test platform: NVIDIA DGX Spark (GB10) · Models: System One family · Report date: November 2026 .

700.title: VLM Inference Benchmark Explorer
700.content: How many cameras can this device watch with this vision-language model? Pick the image size your cameras send and set how long a camera may wait for its answer; the table updates for every configuration we have measured. Expand any row to see its measurements for every number of cameras, the results explained and a chart. How to use the benchmark explorer

701.title: What a row is
701.content: A row is one deployment configuration: a vision-language model, on specific hardware, in a specific number format, served by a specific engine, measured end to end. The same model therefore appears in several rows, and two rows are directly comparable only once you know which of those settings differ between them.

702.title: Filters and the target do different jobs
702.content: Filters decide which rows you see. The device, model, parameter-count, quantization and engine filters, and the TTFT slider, only show or hide rows. The target and the assumption decide what the numbers say. They sit under Performance Target and Assumptions. Changing one leaves the rows in place but recalculates Max Cameras and the green and red colouring of every row.

703.title: 1. Describe your cameras
703.content: Two selectors describe the workload, and every number in the table is read at them: . | Cameras — how many cameras send requests at the same moment. This is the concurrency the system was measured at. | Image Size — the size of each image a camera sends: 480p, 720p, 1080p or 2K. | . Rows not measured at the selected combination are hidden, and dimmed buttons mark combinations that have no measurement. Several cameras were measured at 480p, 720p and 1080p; 2K with one camera only.

704.title: 2. Narrow and sort
704.content: Filters combine, and every column sorts. The most instructive comparisons change a single setting: one model at two quantizations on one device, the same model under llama.cpp and vLLM, or one model on two devices.

705.title: 3. Set your target
705.content: The target is the longest a camera may wait for its answer to start — default 3000 ms. A mean TTFT exactly on the target passes. Beside it, Images per Camera sets how many images each request carries: one snapshot by default, or several frames of the same camera sent together, as video is often sent to a vision-language model. Several images per request were measured with one camera only, so with more than one image Max Cameras cannot be higher than 1.

706.title: 4. Read Max Cameras
706.content: Max Cameras is the highest measured number of cameras at which the mean TTFT of their requests is within your target. A plus — 16+ — means the configuration met the target even at the highest number it was tested with, so its real maximum was not reached. “>3000 ms” — your target — means not even a single camera is answered in time.

707.title: 5. Open a row
707.content: Click a row to see: . | on the left, the measurements at your image size and image count for every number of cameras tested, marked “≤3000 ms” or “>3000 ms” against your target, and closed by the number of cameras that failed where the camera limit was measured, and below them the same for the number of images in one request, with one camera; | on the right, the results explained in plain language, at the default settings; | below, a chart of TTFT as cameras are added, one line per image size, with your target as a dashed line. It appears where several cameras were measured, so with one image per camera. | . The chart downloads as a PNG for reports and presentations.

708.title: Where to start
708.content: “How many cameras can one Jetson AGX Orin 32GB watch?” Select the device, set the image size your cameras send, and read Max Cameras. To see only the configurations that keep up, select the number of cameras you need and set Max TTFT to your target. “Is 1080p worth it?” Switch the image size and watch Max Cameras, or open a row: its chart has one line per image size. “What do quantization and the engine change?” Hold the model and the device fixed and compare the rows that differ in that one setting: Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct at Q8_0 and Q4_K_M on Jetson AGX Orin 32GB, or Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct under llama.cpp and vLLM on RTX PRO 6000. Changing the number of cameras shows how the gap develops under load. “We already own this hardware; what can we run on it?” Start with the device filter, sort the remaining models by size or by Max Cameras, and narrow with the TTFT or the number of cameras you need. What the numbers mean and how they are calculated

709.title: How the numbers were measured
709.content: Each request carries one or more photos and the prompt Describe the scene., and asks for up to 128 tokens. The photos are sixteen fixed pictures, cycled through the requests and scaled to 854×480 (480p), 1280×720 (720p), 1920×1080 (1080p) and 2560×1440 (2K), sent as base64 images through the OpenAI-compatible chat API. Hugging Face checkpoints were served with vLLM and GGUF files with llama.cpp. Every combination of image size, images per request and number of cameras is measured on its own, after a warm-up batch that is discarded. The figures are means of the requests that completed; a request that failed during the benchmark is left out of the mean and does not count against a configuration. | Several cameras were measured with one image per request at 480p, 720p and 1080p: 1, 2 and 4 cameras on Jetson Orin NX 16GB (up to 8 for one configuration), up to 8 on Jetson AGX Orin 32GB and its Developer Kit, and up to 16 on RTX PRO 6000, Jetson AGX Thor and DGX Spark, with 8 requests per level on a Jetson Orin and 24 on the others, never more cameras’ requests in flight than the level. The Jetson Orin configurations served with llama.cpp b11690 were measured at 1, 2, 4 and 8 cameras with 24 requests per level. | One camera was measured at all four sizes with one, three and five images per request (1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 on Jetson AGX Thor and DGX Spark, and for the Jetson Orin configurations served with llama.cpp b11690), 5 requests each (3 for one configuration). 2K and several images per request were measured this way only. | The camera limit was measured on Jetson AGX Thor and DGX Spark, at 720p with one image per camera: 16, 32, 64 and more cameras, two requests per camera, until a request had no answer started within 30 seconds; the range between the last number that passed and the first that failed was then halved until it was at most an eighth of the passing number (at least 4 cameras). The server was set to take every camera’s request at once. A request answered with no text did not count as failed. | The image limit was measured on Jetson AGX Thor and DGX Spark, at 720p with one camera: 64, 128, 256, 512 and 1024 images per request, 3 requests each, until a request failed — too long for the model, or no answer within 600 s. | . A token is the unit a model reads and writes, about three quarters of an English word. An image is read as tokens too, and a larger image becomes more of them.

710.title: TTFT — time to first token
710.content: TTFT (time to first token) is how long a camera waits until its answer starts, in milliseconds; the table shows the mean over the requests measured. For a vision-language model this is mostly reading the images, so it grows with their size and number, and with the number of cameras sharing the device. How much it grows with size depends on the model: some turn every image into a fixed number of tokens, others into more tokens the more pixels there are. Lower is better. TPS (tokens per second) is how fast the answer is then written, per camera. It barely depends on the image, and it is shown for reference: Max Cameras is decided by the TTFT. A long answer adds its writing time on top — 128 tokens at 25 tokens per second take about five more seconds.

711.title: Max Cameras: the number of cameras is the concurrency
711.content: A camera sends its next request as soon as the previous one is answered, so it always has exactly one request in flight. The number of concurrent requests is therefore the number of cameras. Max Cameras is the highest measured number of cameras at which the mean TTFT meets your target. Only measured numbers count, nothing is interpolated, and if none passes the cell shows your target, “>3000 ms”. It depends on your target and moves with it: at 720p with one image per camera, Cosmos3-Edge on Jetson AGX Orin 32GB keeps up with 2 cameras at a 1000 ms target and 8 — the highest number measured, so 8+ — at 3000 ms. Max Images per Request reads the same way for the images one camera sends in a single request: the most that still meet your target. An opened row also gives the configuration’s limits, whatever the target — the camera and image limits described above: the most cameras, and the most images in one request, that still worked before a request failed, and the count that failed. Where no limit was searched it says how far the measurement went. On Jetson AGX Thor and DGX Spark Max Cameras goes past 16 too, up to the camera limit.

712.title: The columns that describe the setup
712.content: Parameters — the model’s total number of weights, vision encoder included, as published. For a mixture-of-experts model this is the total, not the part active for each token, because all of it is held in memory. Quantization — the number format the weights are stored in. BF16 is full precision, FP8 uses 8 bits and NVFP4 4 bits. Q8_0, Q4_K_M and Q4_0 are GGUF formats for llama.cpp with about 8 and 4 bits per weight. Fewer bits means less memory and usually more speed, at some risk to quality. Engine — the server software that loads the model and schedules requests. It affects speed as much as the hardware does. Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct on RTX PRO 6000 at 720p starts answering a single camera after 247 ms under llama.cpp (Q8_0) and 164 ms under vLLM (BF16); at 16 cameras the gap is 1094 ms against 461 ms. Device — Jetson Orin NX 16GB and Jetson AGX Orin 32GB are embedded modules whose CPU and GPU share one memory. Both modules also come in other memory sizes, so the name states the one measured. Jetson AGX Orin 32GB Developer Kit is the developer kit with its own 32 GB module, listed apart from the production module. Jetson AGX Thor (developer kit) and DGX Spark also share one memory between CPU and GPU, 128 GB each. RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell is a workstation GPU with 96 GB, measured in its 600 W Workstation and 300 W Max-Q editions.

It is not a substitute for a test with your own cameras and prompts: other image content, longer prompts or answers, other engine settings and the slowest requests rather than the mean all change real capacity. About this runInkling-2-Mini always reasons before it answers: its chat template has no switch to turn this off, and even the lowest reasoning effort writes a short reasoning first. Its time to first token is therefore the time to its first reasoning token — the images and the prompt are processed by then, as in the other rows — and the 128 output tokens include the reasoning. Measured on a shared server as it was deployed: vLLM 0.34 nightly, DSpark speculative decoding (k=7), 256K context, prefix caching on; every request carried new image pixels, so nothing was reused between requests. The server takes at most 64 requests at once (max-num-seqs 64). At 720p, 256 images in one request were refused by vLLM's own cap on decoded image data per request (about 716 MB; 256 images at 720p are 719 MB), not by GPU memory or context length. Cameras: 120 at 720p got their first token within 30 s; at 128, 36 of 256 requests waited longer — beyond 64 cameras, requests queue for a free slot. Permanent page for this configuration . Driving test: six cameras, TensorRT Edge-LLM recipeAlpamayo2-Edge is a driving model: from six cameras (22 frames), the vehicle's recent motion and a navigation instruction it writes a short chain of causation and plans six candidate trajectories. The table above measures only its vision-language part, served with vLLM in BF16 with greedy decoding, the way the model answers questions. Its answers to "Describe the scene." are short (2 to 48 tokens on average per cell), so its tok/s figures swing more than other rows'. This test runs the whole model with its official FP8 TensorRT Edge-LLM recipe (TensorRT Edge-LLM v0.11.1, 5 diffusion steps, 6 candidates, greedy decoding of the chain of causation) on the recipe's 19 navigation demo clips, 3 runs each. Jetson AGX Thor at MAXN with jetson_clocks and TensorRT 11.3; the recipe's own figures come from a DRIVE AGX Thor with TensorRT 11.3. As in the recipe, each decision encodes only the newest frame of every camera and reuses the earlier ones. With all 22 frames encoded inside the timed run a decision takes 402 ms. TensorRT 11.3 brought the trajectory expert from 99 to 70 ms; fixing the GPU and memory clocks with jetson_clocks (memory at 4266 MHz instead of about 2750) brought the rest. The recipe gives about 7 ms per token for greedy decoding but no greedy total; about 320 ms is its stages plus 22 tokens × 7 ms. In the table above 2 requests came back with an empty answer; as in the camera limit, an empty answer is not counted as a failure, so it does not end a series. There is no TensorRT recipe for this model; attention runs through PyTorch SDPA, because flash-attn has no build for this board. About this runInkling-2-Mini always reasons before it answers: its chat template has no switch to turn this off, and even the lowest reasoning effort writes a short reasoning first. Its time to first token is therefore the time to its first reasoning token — the images and the prompt are processed by then, as in the other rows — and the 128 output tokens include the reasoning. Measured on a shared server as it was deployed: vLLM 0.34 nightly, DSpark speculative decoding (k=7), 256K context, prefix caching on; every request carried new image pixels, so nothing was reused between requests. One request with 32 images at 1080p, and later one with 16 images at 2K, made the DGX Spark stop responding altogether: it dropped off the network and needed a power cycle, with no error in the kernel log. Those are the failure points shown here. For that reason the camera, concurrency and many-image tests were not run on this board; the RTX PRO 6000 row has them for the same model. The server was restarted once during the run, with 75% of the memory for vLLM (gpu-memory-utilization 0.75); 480p and 720p were measured before, 1080p and 2K after.
